text:
The Cooling Shortage Explained by Trading Assistant

@elonmusk is onto something… again…

The US data center industry is facing a severe bottleneck driven by the exponential growth of artificial intelligence. AI workloads require high-density server racks packed with advanced GPUs (like Nvidia’s H100 and B200 series). These chips consume massive amounts of electricity and generate unprecedented heat. 

Traditional air-cooling systems cannot handle the thermal density of modern AI racks. As a result, data centers are being forced to transition to expensive liquid cooling systems. Furthermore, cooling requires massive amounts of power and water—straining local electrical grids and drawing regulatory backlash over the millions of gallons of water consumed daily by cooling towers. Simply put, we are running out of terrestrial power and water to keep AI cold.

How Space Data Centers Play Into This
To bypass terrestrial grid limits and environmental constraints, aerospace and tech companies are exploring "orbital data centers." Moving computation to space offers two massive theoretical advantages:
Infinite Cooling: Deep space is a near-infinite heat sink. While thermal management in orbit is actually quite complex due to direct solar radiation, spacecraft can use passive radiators to dump heat into the vacuum of space without needing millions of gallons of water.
Uninterrupted Power: Satellites in specific orbits can harvest solar energy 24/7 without atmospheric interference, weather disruptions, or day/night cycles, completely bypassing the terrestrial power grid.

Instead of beaming raw data down to Earth to be processed, the idea is to process the data in orbit and only beam down the finished, compressed results. Projects like the European ASCEND feasibility study and startups like Lonestar Data Holdings (which is looking at lunar data centers) are actively exploring this.

Desirable Markets & Beneficiaries
This dynamic creates two distinct investment timelines:

1. The Near-Term Winners: Terrestrial Thermal Management
Before space data centers become viable, the immediate capital is flowing into companies that solve the terrestrial cooling crisis. The shift from air to liquid cooling (direct-to-chip and immersion cooling) makes thermal management infrastructure highly desirable.
Vertiv ($VRT ): A dominant player in data center power and cooling infrastructure.
Modine Manufacturing ($MOD ): A leader in thermal management systems that has pivoted heavily into data center cooling.
nVent Electric ($NVT ): Specializes in liquid cooling solutions and server enclosures.

2. The Long-Term Winners: Space Infrastructure
If orbital computation becomes a reality, the bottleneck shifts from terrestrial real estate to launch capacity and orbital communications.
Launch Providers: SpaceX ($SPCX ) and Rocket Lab ($RKLB ) would be the primary beneficiaries, as deploying massive server farms into orbit requires cheap, frequent heavy-lift capabilities.
Optical Communications: Companies developing laser-based satellite communications will be critical for transmitting high-bandwidth AI data back to Earth.

Current Market Sentiment on Space Data Centers
While the concept is gaining traction, prediction markets show that actual deployment is still viewed as a multi-year project. On Polymarket, the odds of an AI data center launching into space by the end of 2026 are currently priced at just 2% (2¢). However, the market sees it accelerating shortly after, with the odds of a launch by the end of 2027 jumping to 18%. 

Interestingly, there is also a specific Polymarket contract pricing a 12% chance that Google and SpaceX officially announce a partnership for orbital data centers by the end of 2026.

text:
Reimagining World Wrestling Entertainment

World Wrestling Entertainment needs a complete reset: not less wrestling, but a stronger identity built around professional wrestling as a major sporting institution. The model would combine modern production and competitive structure with the principles of Jesse McMahon, Vince J. McMahon Sr. and Toots Mondt: strong local markets, memorable attractions, dependable touring and the ring at the center of the business.

The WWE brand would remain, but the current television ecosystem would end. There would be one unified roster with no brand split, rotating between Monday and Friday broadcasts according to rankings, rivalries and schedules. No Raw. No SmackDown. Just World Wrestling Entertainment.

Madison Square Garden would be WWE’s home turf, serving as its symbolic headquarters, much as Arena México does for CMLL and the Tokyo Dome for NJPW. It would host major title defenses, tournament finals, landmark debuts and historic rivalries. WWE would tour nationally and internationally, but MSG would remain its defining venue.

Following the McMahon tradition, WWE would cultivate regional relationships rather than merely visit cities. Arenas, promoters, wrestling schools and fan communities would become part of a dependable national touring network.

The presentation would be stripped down. Replace the entrance stage with a simple entrance tunnel leading directly to the ring. Television would combine house-show intimacy, boxing and MMA intensity, and independent-wrestling grit: fewer cuts, minimal graphics, natural crowd noise and limited CGI. Blood and profanity would be used sparingly, when they add genuine intensity.

Inspired by Mondt, WWE would emphasize clear stakes, strong finishes and wrestlers capable of carrying a card. Matches would have time limits, rankings and official records. Referees would function like boxing or MMA officials, with authority to enforce rules, stop matches and protect competitors. Outside interference would be prohibited and severely punished. Championships would resemble prestigious sporting trophies, not oversized corporate props.

Tag-team and women’s wrestling would be major attractions, with their own rankings, records, tournaments and championship programs. Either division could headline a broadcast or major event.

The annual calendar would center on Royal Rumble, WrestleMania and SummerSlam, supported by two major tournaments: The Wrestling Classic, a World Cup-style international competition, and King of the Ring, an open, FA Cup-style knockout tournament.

Ohio Valley Wrestling would serve as WWE’s primary developmental system, retaining its identity while training wrestlers in fundamentals, conditioning, psychology, promos and WWE’s competitive rules.

WWE should also learn from Game Changer Wrestling and Major League Wrestling. GCW offers lessons in intimacy, unpredictability and fan connection; MLW shows that “major league” does not require a polished or sanitized product. WWE should be professional, not sterile; major league, not corporate-looking.

Commercialization would remain necessary but secondary. Fans should feel like members of a wrestling community, not targets of constant marketing.

The goal is a distinct North American wrestling culture: sporting seriousness, cultural passion, strong markets, memorable attractions, disciplined touring and respect for the audience.

One WWE. One roster. Madison Square Garden as home turf. Strong local markets. Meaningful competition. Prestigious championships. Serious officiating. Gritty presentation. Fewer distractions. More wrestling.

text:
ALWAYS read the fine print. I learnt this one the hard way. 

I wanted a nice dining table. Searched online and Coco Luxury Furniture came up. Zoomed off there with excitement.

Saw exactly what I wanted. Marble table, 6 chairs. $3,699.

They told me they offer interest free credit if I pay it off within a certain time. I mean, why cough out $3,699 at once when you can spread it at 0%? I accepted.

They linked me to American First Finance. Checked my payslips, my bank account, everything. Said I qualified for $7K+. I only needed $3,699.

Now here's where I went wrong. This wasn't my first time buying like this. I did the same thing at Mattress Firm in South Carolina. About $5K mattress, they linked me to Synchrony Bank, monthly debits, 0% interest. Smooth.

So I assumed Texas would be the same. I didn't read the contract.

March, the debits start. $334.13 every two weeks, and it lands on payday.

July, I logged into the AFF portal just to see how far I had gone. Two more payments and I would have covered the full $3,699.

Then I saw something on the side. EPO. $7,472.

I said how?

Went and dug up the contract from my email. What I saw shocked me.

It was not credit. It was a LEASE TO OWN.

"You do not own the Property... You do not obtain any ownership rights until you have paid for the Property in full by making 104 weekly, 52 bi-weekly... for a total of $15,733.69."

$15,733.69. For a table that costs $3,699.

That is when it clicked. There is no interest rate anywhere in that document. None. Because legally you are renting, not borrowing, so the interest caps don't apply.

I had a trip out of the country coming up so I left it. When I came back I engaged a law firm through my  legal plan.

Their advice? Before we escalate, go and talk to them yourself first.

Best advice I got. I called AFF and negotiated.

We settled at $2,000 instead of $7,472.

Final damage: $6,063.69 on a $3,699 table.

Still lost money. But not $15,733.

What I learnt:

"Interest free if you pay early" is not the same as 0% financing. Ask them straight: is this a loan or a lease?
No APR on the paper means it is not credit.

Call and negotiate before you accept whatever number is on the screen. They came down by $5,400.

Don't be me. Please read your fine print.

text:
Bessent vs. Bessent: How the U.S. Treasury Secretary Became an Inverted Version of Himself

Scott Bessent spent years as a macro investor who bet against central bank interventions in the markets — and now, as Treasury Secretary, he himself is intervening aggressively in the bond market to suppress yields. The sharpest criticism comes precisely from his former mentor, Stanley Druckenmiller. What's behind the reversal, and what is the broader economic plan Bessent is promoting?

With a few perfectly plausible twists, we might find ourselves today with Scott Bessent, the energetic Treasury Secretary of the Trump administration, as chairman of the Federal Reserve. He is one of the most respected figures in the economic world, with a deep understanding of macroeconomics and monetary and fiscal policy.

He built a career as a successful investor and hedge fund manager precisely on the strength of this understanding. As is well known, Bessent was a key partner in George Soros's famous attack that broke the British pound in 1992, netting the Quantum Fund a profit of a billion dollars. Another, less well-known but no less successful move was his short position against the Japanese yen in 2013, which earned the fund a profit of over a billion dollars in just three months.

These moves show a results-driven investor with a killer instinct, but also one who understands deeply how central banks function, their capabilities, and — more importantly — their limitations and weaknesses.

In fact, the hedge fund he founded in 2015, following the great successes at Quantum Fund, was built on the premise that in a world where central banks intervene deeply in markets through interest rates and massive liquidity injections, a macro player must deeply understand the political and economic motives and constraints of decision-makers in order to anticipate the market's next moves — and profit from them.

A Decade of Ups and Downs: What Bessent's Real Track Record as an Investor Looks Like

The hedge fund he founded did not meet expectations, and as an independent manager he struggled to maintain consistent returns. After a relatively successful first year, the fund he managed went through a rather difficult period between 2017 and 2021, during which it stagnated and, according to some reports, even recorded cumulative losses. The main reason was a strongly bullish market environment in which macro players seeking trend reversals or crises struggled badly against central banks' expansionary monetary policy. The lack of success led to a significant decline in assets under management as institutional investors pulled their money.

Despite the asset erosion, the fund's recent years (especially 2022 and 2024) were highly profitable and salvaged much of Bessent's reputation as a sharp macro investor, just before its complete closure in favor of his move to political and public life. In 2022, a year of sharp declines across the board, Bessent reportedly posted a significant profit of over 30%. In 2024 too, the fund recorded a double-digit profit thanks to favorable positions around the election results (the Trump rally).

When the Treasury Starts Acting Like a Central Bank

The fund's partial success under his management did not damage Bessent's reputation as an outstanding economist with extensive macro knowledge and a deep understanding of the relationship between the central bank and the markets. Against this reputational backdrop, more than a few eyebrows were raised on Wall Street regarding Bessent's aggressive moves in the bond market — particularly the decision to dramatically expand buyback programs for long-term government bonds in order to bring down yields that had spiked to levels difficult to sustain.

The arguments against the intervention sound quite similar to what Bessent the investor would likely have said about Bessent the Treasury Secretary.

Direct intervention in the bond market to influence long-term yields is an exclusive tool of the central bank within the framework of monetary policy. When the Treasury Department uses its cash reserves to carry out aggressive bond purchases aimed at pushing yields downward, it is effectively engaging in "market engineering" or fiscal price manipulation. This action blurs the line between fiscal policy (the government's management of budget, taxes, and debt) and monetary policy (the central bank's control over interest rates and the money supply).

Bessent's move essentially puts the Treasury Department at odds with the Fed and Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. While the Fed weighs its steps to ensure inflation doesn't rear its head again and maintains relatively tight market conditions, the Treasury Department is actively moving in the opposite direction — trying to ease credit conditions and lower financing costs for the government and for citizens (such as mortgages).

The Student Versus the Teacher

The sharpest criticism of Bessent comes precisely from those most similar to him — chief among them his longtime mentor, billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller. Druckenmiller came out against the artificial suppression of yields, arguing that "every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination" of genuine fiscal reforms. In his view, the bond market is meant to serve as a "gatekeeper" that sends warnings to the government about ballooning deficits and unsustainable debt. When the Treasury intervenes to paper over the problem and force yields down, it hides the "economic truth" from the public and from politicians, and encourages reckless fiscal behavior.

Another argument is that when a player like the Treasury Department sets a ceiling or floor on bond prices, it damages the credibility of the world's largest debt market. Institutional investors may lose confidence in the mechanism by which prices reflect real supply and demand, which over the long term could produce the opposite effect — driving investors away or demanding a higher "risk premium" on American debt due to the uncertainty created by a market that isn't functioning freely.

So Why Did the Hedge Fund Tiger Change Its Stripes?

Against the backdrop of this criticism, Bessent's sharp transition from "private macro trader" who bets against central bank distortions, to "policy captain" who himself tries to bend the market and produces what looks like similar distortions, seems somewhat strange and requires explanation.

The simple explanation for why Treasury Secretary Bessent is pursuing a policy he himself would probably have bet against had he still been a private investor is not that he denies the depth of the fiscal problem — but that he disagrees about the right way to solve it. While critics, led by Druckenmiller, argue that high yields are a "truth alarm" the market is sending about an unsustainable debt trajectory, and that the only remedy is immediate, painful fiscal restraint, Bessent himself does not deny the diagnosis.

In his speech at the G20 summit in Asheville, North Carolina (a speech we'll return to later), he openly acknowledged that "the world is awash in debt" since the global financial crisis and the Covid crisis, but immediately added that "the only way out of this is to grow our way out of it." Bessent even described the role he has taken on in his own dramatic terms: "Sometimes I feel like an emergency room doctor, and the economy is the patient, and the American people were run over by the Biden truck," he said, adding that "we've stabilized the patient, and now we're in the healing phase."

In other words: the deficit is indeed structural and deep, but Bessent rejects the prescription of sharp cuts. In his view, fiscal austerity amid a high-yield environment would only choke off the growth meant to solve the problem in the first place, creating a negative spiral of slowdown that worsens the debt-to-GDP ratio rather than improving it. The solution he offers lies not in shrinking demand but in expanding supply: aggressive growth driven by deregulation, energy, and investment, that would grow GDP faster than the debt grows.

From this perspective, the long-term solution isn't found in the bond market itself but somewhere else entirely — in aggressive growth that would reduce the debt burden relatively, even if not absolutely. That is, even if the nominal debt keeps growing, as long as the growth rate outpaces the rate of debt growth, the debt-to-GDP ratio — the truly meaningful figure for fiscal stability — remains under control and even improves over time.

The problem is that the current situation creates a kind of vicious circle: yields that are too high make financing more expensive for both the government and the private sector, thereby constituting in themselves a significant barrier to the growth that is supposed to solve the debt problem in the first place. From this stems, in Bessent's approach, the justification for targeted and timed intervention in the bond market — not as a permanent substitute for responsible fiscal policy, but as a temporary bridge meant to keep financing costs at a bearable level until structural reforms and the growth they're meant to produce begin to bear fruit. Bessent's push for a policy that favors growth over regulation is not incidental — it constitutes a direct application of a neoliberal economic worldview reminiscent of the principles of "Reaganomics" from the 1980s.

Therefore, this move should be viewed against the backdrop of the Treasury Secretary's broader policy, which is based on an ideology of supply-side economics, the pragmatism of a macro trader, and a deep understanding of how financial markets (particularly the bond and currency markets) respond to signals from governments.

3-3-3: The Plan Meant to Save the American Economy

The central principles through which Bessent's macro thesis manifests in official policy unfold across several parallel arenas.

The first of these is the "3-3-3" strategy for growth and fiscal policy: a structured economic plan Bessent has formulated and promotes, reflecting the approach of a macro investor trying to stabilize a large system.

The first component is 3% GDP growth, emphasizing the removal of bureaucratic obstacles to accelerate organic economic activity, based on the belief that real growth is the best way to "grow out of" national debt.

The second component is reducing the deficit to 3% of GDP, through restraint in government spending and increased efficiency to bring the fiscal deficit down to sustainable levels by 2028, thereby calming the bond markets and preventing pressure on long-term bond yields (currently, with a deficit at 5.8% of GDP, this is far from the target).

The third component is increasing American oil and gas output by an amount equivalent to an additional 3 million barrels of oil per day, aimed at lowering energy prices for consumers and industry. This point connects directly to the next principle in his thesis.

Controlling Energy Prices: As someone who has analyzed commodity prices and their impact on global inflation for years, Bessent sees broad domestic energy production as the key to lowering the cost of living. Unlike the pure monetary approach, which argues that only raising Federal Reserve interest rates can curb inflation, Bessent believes that increasing energy supply lowers costs across the entire economy without choking off growth.

The tariffs issue may at first glance seem like an element that contradicts this entire neoliberal approach. However, Bessent sees tariffs not as a one-dimensional protectionist tool, but as a tactical negotiating tool in the arsenal of macro-politics. Their purpose is to create more balanced trade conditions, encourage the return of manufacturing plants to the United States, and fund tax cuts for domestic businesses — all with the goal of encouraging sustainable growth that relies on production as well as consumption.

Finally, one of the great lessons of a veteran macro trader is that you can't fight the bond market. Bessent is well aware that massive deficits can send government bond yields soaring and harm the economy. Therefore, his Treasury policy places heavy emphasis on credible signals to the world's largest institutional investors, in order to maintain market confidence in the stability of American debt — and thereby calm the bond market's "vigilantes."

Ultimately, the central goal of all this is to encourage sustainable, long-term growth. Such growth could lower long-term bond yields, keep the fiscal debt under control, and do all this without significant inflation — almost a utopian dream of a perfect economy.

Bessent to the World: Get Back to Basics

An interesting glimpse into Bessent's ideology could be gained from his aggressive speech at the G20 summit, where he preached the core tenets of "supply-side economics," arguing that this is the right approach not only for the United States but for all the world's leading economies.

At the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors summit that opened this week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took center stage and delivered a combative, uncompromising opening speech before the finance ministers and central bank governors of the world's leading economies. He called on global decision-makers to "get back to basics," and stressed that the world must abandon cumbersome regulatory policy and refocus on encouraging free enterprise and business expansion.

According to Bessent, the international economic system has suffered in recent years from excessive regulatory burden, choking bureaucracy, and unwieldy fiscal and monetary policy that severely harm the growth potential of leading economies. In his speech, the Treasury Secretary made clear that the United States under the Trump administration would push an agenda that puts growth first, prioritizing the removal of barriers, reducing the tax burden, and encouraging private investment as the central response to threats of inflation and global slowdown.

Bessent's remarks mark a notable shift in America's tone on the international stage, and signal to G20 nations that Washington expects them to fall in line with a policy of freer markets, seeking to accelerate business activity by freeing the private sector from the shackles of public institutions.

According to Bessent, since the subprime crisis of 2008 and later the Covid crisis, the global financial system has experienced an unprecedented wave of regulatory tightening, including various Basel banking regulations, stricter reporting requirements, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) regulations, and greater government involvement in markets.

These steps, though intended to produce stability and prevent systemic crises, have in practice become a heavy weight burdening small and large companies alike, reducing market liquidity and artificially inflating costs for the end consumer. Bessent, who grew up in the world of investment and private fund management, brings to the discussion table a distinctly business-oriented perspective, holding that the only way to deal with high sovereign debts and persistent inflation is by expanding the economic pie through productivity and entrepreneurship — not by shrinking demand or imposing new restrictions on the business sector.

The American Treasury Secretary's call places the representatives of the various G20 nations — including the United States, European Union countries, China, Japan, Britain, and other major emerging economies — before a highly complex policy and economic dilemma. On one hand, many markets around the world, particularly in Europe, continue to cling to rigid regulatory agendas, whether in the field of green energy, consumer protection, or tight technological oversight of digital giants. On the other hand, the marked slowdown in China's economic growth rate, alongside the fiscal pressures characterizing most Western nations, necessitate a rethinking of the engines driving the global economy.

Bessent's remarks may serve as a catalyst for charged discussions at the current summit, as they challenge the international consensus that has prevailed in recent years around the need for broad government intervention. For investors on Wall Street and in leading exchanges worldwide, the message from Washington is generally received favorably, as it promises a more business-friendly environment, less bureaucracy, and the prospect of future tax relief; however, it also raises questions about international cooperation on critical issues such as oversight of global financial risks, the fight against climate change, and the prevention of trade wars, since an agenda promoting aggressive national growth could lead to new inter-bloc clashes on the international economic stage.

In Conclusion

Ultimately, Scott Bessent's paradox is also his most compelling story: the man who built an entire career on identifying the moments when central banks and governments try to bend the market instead of listening to it, now finds himself doing exactly that. The question that will determine whether his move will be remembered as a triumph or a failure isn't technical but temporal: will the growth he's promising arrive fast enough to justify the intervention in the bond market — before investors, led by his own longtime teacher, decide they're no longer willing to wait.

text:
Look past the handshake in Bishkek.

China Russia India Pakistan and Iran sat in the same room this week while two wars still burn. Ukraine after four and a half years. Iran after six months of fire with Washington and Tel Aviv. The SCO is twenty five years old and suddenly it looks like half the planet found a table that does not need a Western chair.

That is the photograph. The story underneath is colder.

This is not a unified camp against America. India will take Russian oil and Russian arms and still tell Putin the world must leave endless war behind. Modi will greet Pezeshkian and talk peace while refusing to become a junior partner in a Beijing Moscow bloc. China wants corridors and cash gravity. Central Asia wants the money without becoming a province. Pakistan sits across from India and both pretend the air is normal. Kyrgyzstan wants funds and railways and a moment on the map.

Putin offered China permanent visa free travel after tourism jumped forty three percent. Xi talks global governance. Guterres is in the building. Erdogan hovers at the edge. Speeches will fill the Bishkek Declaration. Watch three things instead. The language they can all live with on terrorism and the Iran war. Who actually gets time with whom. Whether any real money moves.

Orders do not shift because leaders hug. They shift when gas routes financing and ports change hands. These capitals do not trust each other. They showed up anyway. That is the news.

text:
Pat Tillman was the 226th pick in the 1998 draft. Seventh round. An undersized safety out of Arizona State who was supposed to be a camp body.

By 2000 he held the Arizona Cardinals franchise record with 224 tackles in a season.

In 2001, the St. Louis Rams offered him more money than Arizona was paying. He turned it down and stayed with the Cardinals, a team that had won nothing, because he felt loyal to them.

Then September 11th happened.

In May 2002, Tillman turned down a three year, $3.6 million contract extension from Arizona and enlisted in the United States Army alongside his younger brother Kevin, who gave up a minor league baseball career to do it.

Army salary at the time was roughly $18,000 a year.

They took the oath together at a recruiting station in Chandler, Arizona, on May 31, 2002. Both became Rangers, assigned to the 2nd Battalion of the 75th Ranger Regiment, based at Fort Lewis, Washington.

Here is the part almost nobody mentions.

Pat Tillman never explained himself. Not once.

Every network wanted the interview. He turned down all of them. He gave no speeches, wrote no op-eds, made no appearances. He specifically did not want to be a recruiting poster or a symbol for anything.

Friends said 9/11 affected him deeply. That's as close to a public reason as anyone ever got, and it came from other people, not him.

He deployed to Iraq in 2003, then Afghanistan in 2004.

On April 22, 2004, he was killed near the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. He was 27.

The Army told his family, and the country, that he died in an enemy ambush. The story that went out was that he charged up a hill toward insurgent fire to protect his unit. He was posthumously awarded the Silver Star for gallantry against enemy fire. A nationally televised memorial was built around that account.

Five weeks later, the Pentagon told the Tillman family that none of it was true.

Pat Tillman was killed by his own unit. Shot three times in the head by American fire in a confused firefight after a friendly Afghan soldier near him was mistakenly targeted.

Soldiers who were there had known within days.

What came out afterward is worse than the mistake itself. Investigations found that witness statements had been altered. His uniform and body armor were burned. His personal diary was destroyed, against regulations. The Silver Star narrative describing enemy fire was written and approved by people who already suspected fratricide.

In 2007, the Army censured retired three-star general Philip Kensinger, who ran special operations at the time, for lying to investigators.

His mother, Mary Tillman, a schoolteacher, spent years going through boxes of documents that arrived nearly black with redactions, trying to piece together how her son actually died. She never got a full answer about who wrote the false narrative.

"It's happening to other soldiers," she said. "It's a systemic problem."

His father put it more bluntly about why the truth came out at all.

"They crossed the wrong family."

Here's why the way we remember him matters.

Pat Tillman was a person, not a slogan. He was an atheist. He read constantly, everything from Emerson to writers who disagreed with everything the government was doing. He kept a journal. He asked hard questions and by his family's account he did not like everything he saw once he was in.

He turned down millions of dollars and he refused to tell anyone why, because he didn't think his choice made him better than the working class kids getting shipped out alongside him.

Then he died, and within days the institution he served built a story about him that wasn't true, because the real one was inconvenient.

The number 40 hangs retired in Arizona. His foundation has put thousands of veterans and military spouses through school.

The most honest thing anyone can say about Pat Tillman is that he never asked to be a symbol, and he isn't around to correct the ones we made of him.

🇷🇺🇨🇳🇮🇳 India and Pakistan, China and India, all seated at the same table in Kyrgyzstan this week.

The SCO is 25: Ten members, roughly half the planet. China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus, and Central Asia are meeting while Ukraine still burns and Iran is at war. 

Guterres is there, and Erdoğan is around the edges. This is no longer a quiet regional club.

The SCO is often described as a counterweight to Washington, but it isn’t a unified anti-U.S. bloc: its members have competing strategic interests, different relationships with the West and, in some cases, longstanding tensions with each other.

That makes the summit significant, as China and Russia may want a more multipolar world with less U.S. dominance, while countries like India have strong incentives to preserve strategic independence rather than simply choose one geopolitical camp.

On Monday, China and Russia pledged to push the SCO toward a bigger role in “global governance,” where Putin offered to make Russia-China visa-free travel permanent after tourism jumped 43%. 

Meanwhile, India is playing a different game. 

Modi hugged Putin, invited him to BRICS in New Delhi, and still told him the world has to leave “endless war” behind. He told Iran’s Pezeshkian India will back efforts at lasting peace. 

Translation: keep Russia for energy and defense, refuse to join a China-Russia camp, talk to everyone.

That is the real summit; India and Pakistan in one room, China and India with an open border dispute, Iran hunting cover, Central Asia wanting Chinese cash without becoming a Chinese province, and Kyrgyzstan trying to turn anniversary talk into funds, corridors, and counterterror machinery.

The SCO cannot replace the West, but they can watch three things: whether the Bishkek Declaration names terrorism and the Iran war in language everyone can live with; who actually gets time with whom; and whether any real money moves. 

Speeches are cheap, but routes, gas, and financing are how an order shifts.

These guys ultimately may not trust each other... but they showed up anyway.

text:
September is Poshan Maah.
It is an opportunity to understand nutrition better, improve our everyday food choices, and contribute towards a healthier, malnutrition-free India.

This year’s focus is on supporting brain development during the first six years of life.

A child’s development does not begin when school starts. The foundation is built much earlier through nutrition, responsive care, adequate sleep, play, learning opportunities, and regular growth monitoring.

Good nutrition does not require expensive powders, imported foods, or a single “superfood.”

Simple, local and seasonal foods such as dal, rice, vegetables, curd, ragi, chana, eggs and other protein-rich options can be an important part of a child’s diet when offered in an age-appropriate form, with adequate variety and consistency.

This Poshan Maah, we will talk about:

* Early-childhood nutrition.
* Complementary feeding.
* Anaemia prevention.
* Common nutrient deficiencies.
* The importance of iodised salt.
* Better cooking practices.
* Healthier snack choices.

This September, let’s make nutrition more practical, more inclusive and more intentional.

Save this Reel and share it with a parent, grandparent or caregiver.

This content is for nutrition awareness and does not replace individual medical or dietetic advice.

If you were the Sabre's GM would you trade for Connor Hellebuyck or is he not worth it.  What would be a fair price in trade for him.

Thought for 38s

I would not do the deal if Winnipeg insists on two high-upside forwards plus a first. The Sabre's long-term strength is their young skaters. Mortgage that for a goalie whose best years may already be behind him and you risk becoming Winnipeg 2.0 — good regular-season team that cannot get over the hump. Hellebuyck is worth it as an upgrade that accelerates a contending window. He is not worth blowing up the future to get. Talks have already happened and he wants Buffalo; the leverage is not entirely with Winnipeg anymore. Make a competitive but disciplined offer and be prepared to walk.Yes, I would pursue it — but only at a price that does not gut Buffalo’s young core. Hellebuyck is still one of the best goalies of his generation, and the Sabres’ window is opening. He is not worth an overpay given his age, last season’s dip, and five years remaining on the deal.nhl.comHellebuyck is 33 with a 7-year, $8.5 million AAV contract that runs through 2030-31 (five years left). He has a full no-movement clause this season. He won the Vezina in 2020, 2024, and 2025, the Hart in 2024-25, and Olympic gold in 2026 with outstanding numbers (1.18 GAA, .956 SV% in five games). Career regular-season numbers are excellent: 345 wins, 45 shutouts, .916 SV%, 2.58 GAA.nhl.comThe 2025-26 season was a clear step back: 23-23-11, 2.86 GAA, .895 SV% in 57 games after mid-November knee surgery. Playoff history is mixed at best (24-34, 2.90 GAA, .903 SV% in 58 games), with some very poor recent series. Goalies typically peak in their late 20s; committing five more years into his late 30s carries real https://t.co/QOD3vo3cXL Why it makes sense for Buffalo The Sabre's finally broke their playoff drought in 2025-26 (50-23-9, 109 points, Atlantic title) with a high-powered offense and a surprisingly effective Luukkonen-Lyon tandem. They still lack a proven, workhorse No. 1 who can steal a series. Adding Hellebuyck would immediately make them a more credible Eastern Conference threat. He has already indicated willingness to waive his NMC for Buffalo.nytimes.comCap-wise it is workable. Buffalo has roughly $5.1 million in space. Sending Luukkonen ($4.75 million AAV through 2028-29) the other way creates a manageable net increase.puckpedia.comLuukkonen (27) just posted a strong regular season (22-9-3, 2.52 GAA, .909 SV% in 35 games) but was ordinary in the playoffs. He is a useful piece, not an untouchable franchise goalie.Fair trade priceJets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff is looking for help up front and a replacement goalie. He will ask high because Hellebuyck is still a name brand with term. Buffalo should not meet an inflated ask.A reasonable framework:Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen (starting goalie they can plug in immediately)
One established young NHL forward who is not a core piece (Jack Quinn or Jiri Kulich)
A first-round pick (2027) or a strong prospect defenseman (not Daxon Rudolph or a top-pair guy)
Possibly a mid-round pick or extra prospect as a sweetener
That package gives Winnipeg a 27-year-old goalie on a team-friendly deal plus scoring help and draft capital. It does not include Zach Benson, Konsta Helenius, or the best defensive prospects. Packages that start with Helenius + Kulich + Luukkonen are too expensive for a 33-year-old coming off a down https://t.co/2qdKva9tjo

text:
Ashwatthama of Mahabharata- mysterious sightings

Ashwatthama had received a curse from Bhagwan Shri Krishna Himself when Bhagwan punished Him by destroying the shining mani (jewel) on Ashwatthama's forehead with His Sudarshana Chakra. This is because the evil Ashwatthama had committed the worst of sins or Paap karmas as the night massacre of the Pandava camp (including Draupadi’s sons) of trying to kill an unborn child, the unborn son of Abhimanyu in Uttara's womb, by invoking the terrible Brahmastra which was a nuclear weapon and directing it on Uttara's womb.

After punishing Ashwatthama, Bhagwan Shri Krishna cursed him that he will remain immortal till the end of Kaliyuga, and the septic wound on his forehead will keep bleeding, pus will keep coming from the wound and it will smell obnoxious, it will pain so much that every moment he will feel like dying but he will not die.

This, Ashwatthama of being a Chiranjeev (immortal), is always sighted atleast once in some form, by the devotee during this Parikrama. 

People in all the earlier Yugas before Kaliyuga had a towering height, average height being 7 feet then.

Multiple instances from Narmada Parikrama pilgrims and locals suggest sightings of Ashwatthama near the Narmada River, particularly in the dense forests of the Shoolpaneshwar wildlife sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh/Gujarat, and near the Asirgarh fort. He is described as a tall figure (over 7ft) with a bleeding, septic forehead wound, and is asking for oil or medicine to cure his wound. 

Sometimes he is sighted in the form of a small fair child with a divine demeanour and bearing wearing only a koupinam vastra and having a bleeding wound on his forehead, during this Yatra.

Accounts claim he appears, asks for oil or herbal remedies, and then vanishes or becomes difficult to trace. Some believe he wanders the jungles during the day and visits a local Shiva temple to offer flowers at night.

Some reports by people also connects his presence to the Khaireshwar temple near Kanpur or Lakhimpur, though the Narmada belt is the most commonly cited area.

Notable Reported sightings and Traditions-

1) By Prithviraj Chauhan (c. 1192 CE) 
After the second Battle of Tarain, the king (himself described as a physician) met an old man with a large, horrible scar on his head in the jungle. Treatments failed for weeks. When asked if he was Ashwatthama, the man confirmed and left. This appears in the 12th-century Prithviraj Raso.0

2) Vaidya in Madhya Pradesh (modern, undated but widely circulated) 
A man arrived with a deep, unusual forehead wound described as looking as if “his brains were pulled out.” The Vaidya joked that the wound seemed ageless—“Are you Ashwatthama?”—and the man vanished from the cabin without being seen leaving. 

3) Railway employee, Navsari jungles, Gujarat (newspaper report, ~20+ years ago)
 While on leave, he encountered a very tall man (claimed ~12 feet) with a wound on his head. They conversed; the man said Bhima was even taller and stronger.3

4) Pilot Baba (20th century) 
He claimed to have met Ashwatthama in the Himalayan foothills, living among tribes and offering daily prayers at a Shiva temple. Details appear in his book "Himalaya Kah Raha Hai".

5) Vasudevanand Saraswati (Tembe Swami, 1912) 
In the dense forest of Shoolpaneshwar (near Katarkheda), Swami an Avataar of Shri Dattatreya Himself, met a man who identified himself as Ashwatthama from the Dvapara Yuga. 

6). Asirgarh Fort (Madhya Pradesh)

This ancient fort is surrounded by dense forests and eerie silence. It houses a Gupteshwar Mahadev temple, where locals believe Ashwatthama comes daily to worship Lord Shiva. Some even say they’ve seen a tall, wounded man walking the grounds.

7).Kalinjar Fort (U.P)
Known for its historical and mythological importance, Kalinjar Fort is often linked to divinity. Locals say Ashwatthama’s presence can still be felt in the old temple ruins and caves.

Making flower garlands has been one of my favourite things since childhood. I used to make huge garlands for the temple near my home and offer them every Saturday evening.
I had such a beautiful, innocent belief back then. I truly believed that after the temple closed on Saturday nights, God would come to the temple. So, I would make sure to offer my garland only after 8:00 p.m., thinking that when He arrived, my garland would be the first thing He would see.
I carried this little belief with me for so many years—almost until I finished my graduation. Looking back now, it makes me smile. It was such a simple, innocent world I lived in, where making a garland with my own hands felt like a personal way of reaching God. Those childhood beliefs may have changed with time, but the sweetness of that memory remains. 
Last Friday, due to Friday pooja, I prepared garlands for diety 👇

text:
The Girl Who Arrived Late — And Changed Ballet Forever

Long before Misty Copeland stood beneath the lights of the American Ballet Theatre, she was a thirteen-year-old girl trying to sleep on the floor of a motel room.

Around her were her mother and five siblings.

There was little space. Little privacy. Little certainty about what would happen next.

For years, Misty's family had moved from place to place. An apartment they could barely afford. A motel room. The home of a friend or relative. Wherever her mother could find a place for six children to stay.

Misty Copeland was born on September 10, 1982, in Kansas City, Missouri. Her father left the family when she was very young, and her mother, Sylvia, was left with the overwhelming responsibility of raising six children.

Financial hardship followed the family for much of Misty's childhood.

At one point, they were living at the Sunset Inn in San Pedro, California. Misty was thirteen years old.

No one could have looked at that crowded motel room and predicted what was coming.

No one could have known that the girl sleeping on the floor would one day help transform one of the world's most exclusive art forms.

Ballet had not been part of Misty's childhood.

She had not grown up attending dance academies. She had never spent years practicing in front of a studio mirror. She did not own ballet shoes.

In fact, ballet barely existed in her world.

Then, at San Pedro High School, Misty joined the drill team.

Something about her movements caught her coach's attention.

She possessed remarkable balance and control. Her movements were unusually graceful. She seemed naturally aware of what her body could do.

The suggestion came simply:

Why not try ballet?

For Misty, it seemed like a world meant for other people.

Ballet required lessons. Equipment. Time. Money.

She had very little of any of those things.

But a free class at a local Boys & Girls Club gave her a chance to step inside a ballet studio for the first time.

She borrowed a pair of shoes.

She approached the barre.

And something extraordinary happened.

Her teachers immediately recognized an unusual natural gift.

Misty was thirteen years old — an age when many aspiring professional dancers had already trained for most of their lives.

Yet she learned with remarkable speed.

One teacher after another began to realize that she possessed something impossible to teach.

Talent.

She still faced a problem, however.

Her life outside the studio was unstable.

Serious ballet training demanded routine, concentration, and countless hours of practice. Misty's home life offered very little stability. Eventually, one of her teachers and that teacher's family offered her the chance to live with them.

For the first time, Misty had her own bedroom.

She had regular meals.

She had a more predictable daily life.

And she had room to dance.

She worked relentlessly to make up for the years she had missed.

The dancers around her had begun as small children. Misty had arrived as a teenager with almost no formal experience.

She had to catch up quickly.

And she did.

Her rise was astonishing. Within only a few years, she was performing and competing at a level that made people take notice.

But talent did not protect her from prejudice.

Ballet had a long-established image of what a ballerina was supposed to look like.

Misty did not fit it.

People criticized her muscular build. They questioned her curves. They suggested that her body did not belong in classical ballet.

There was another difference that could not be ignored.

Misty was Black in a world where Black female dancers had historically been severely underrepresented.

As her career accelerated, her personal life became complicated once again. A painful legal dispute developed between her mother and the family with whom she had been living, and Misty eventually returned to her mother's care.

Yet by then, her future in dance was becoming impossible to deny.

She earned scholarships and continued attracting attention.

At eighteen, she joined the American Ballet Theatre in New York — one of the most prestigious ballet companies in the world.

The road ahead was still difficult.

Questions about her body continued.

Questions about her background continued.

And some continued to focus on the fact that she had begun ballet years later than almost every dancer around her.

Misty kept going.

In 2007, she became a soloist.

Eight years later, her name entered history.

In 2015, at the age of thirty-two, Misty Copeland became the first Black woman to be promoted to principal dancer in the American Ballet Theatre's 75-year history.

A principal dancer is among the highest ranks a ballet performer can achieve.

But her promotion meant more than a title.

For generations, young dancers had rarely seen someone who looked like Misty standing at the center of classical ballet.

Now they could.

She went on to perform some of the most famous roles in ballet and became the first Black woman to dance the leading role of Odette/Odile in Swan Lake with American Ballet Theatre.

Her influence soon extended beyond the stage.

Misty wrote books.

She encouraged young people to pursue dance.

She spoke openly about representation and the narrow standards that had excluded so many people from ballet.

And she refused to pretend that her differences were weaknesses.

The strength people once criticized became part of what made her unforgettable.

The body some believed was wrong for ballet carried her into history.

The late start that was supposed to end her dream became proof that extraordinary potential does not always follow a conventional schedule.

Misty once spoke about wanting to become the person she wished she had been able to see when she was younger.

That may be the greatest measure of her legacy.

A thirteen-year-old girl once slept on a motel floor, uncertain about where life would take her next.

Years later, she stood on one of ballet's most celebrated stages as a principal dancer.

Between those two moments were poverty, instability, prejudice, criticism, legal conflict, and years of relentless work.

But she continued.

She was told she had begun too late.

She was told her body did not fit the tradition.

She entered a world that had rarely made space for someone like her.

And instead of changing herself to fit the old image of a ballerina, Misty Copeland helped change the image itself.

Her story is not simply about a dancer who achieved success against difficult odds.

It is about what happens when opportunity finally reaches someone whose talent might otherwise have remained unseen.

The girl who once had no place of her own eventually claimed her place in history.

And by doing so, she made it easier for countless others to imagine themselves there, too.

Sometimes the most powerful barrier you break is not the one in front of you.

It is the one you remove for everyone who comes after.

Revolutions are usually remembered for the dramatic moment when an old government falls, but what happens afterward is often even more important. 

The first months and years of a new regime reveal how its leaders intend to govern, how they respond to opposition, and whether the promises made during the struggle for power survive once power has actually been won. 

The Russian Revolution is one of history's most revealing examples. It began with enormous hopes for political and social change, yet the political landscape shifted with remarkable speed as new institutions emerged and old freedoms disappeared. 

Historians continue to study this period because it offers a fascinating look at how revolutionary governments consolidate authority and how the balance between security, ideology, and individual liberty can change in a surprisingly short period of time.

Congress Reopens the CIA's MKULTRA Files as Witnesses Call for Answers
Congress revisited the program as calls for more file declassification and answers into unanswered questions remain decades later.
Military Daily News
Published Jul 6, 2026, 5:00 AM EDT
More than four decades after Congress last took a deep look at the CIA’s infamous MKULTRA program, lawmakers are once again asking how much the public still doesn’t know.

The House Oversight Committee’s Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets held a hearing June 30 titled “Mind Control and Accountability: Uncovering the Truth of the CIA’s MKULTRA Project.” The hearing revisited one of the Cold War’s most controversial intelligence programs while examining whether decades of document destruction and government secrecy have prevented a full accounting of what happened.

Witnesses included Stephen Kinzer, a senior fellow at Brown University and author of Poisoner in Chief; investigative journalist Tom O'Neill, author of Chaos: Charles Manson, the CIA, and the Secret History of the Sixties; and Dr. Elizabeth Ginexi, a former National Institutes of Health official who appeared as the minority witness.

Much of the hearing focused on whether additional MKULTRA records still exist and whether victims have ever received meaningful accountability.

What Was MKULTRA?
MKULTRA was a CIA research program launched in 1953 to study methods of influencing or controlling human behavior.

At its peak, MKULTRA encompassed 149 known subprojects carried out at more than 80 institutions, including military bases, universities, hospitals, prisons and pharmaceutical companies.

The CIA frequently used front organizations to conceal its involvement while researchers experimented with drugs such as LSD, mescaline, psilocybin, amphetamines and scopolamine. Some experiments combined those drugs with hypnosis, electroshock therapy, sensory deprivation and isolation.

The program also included safe houses that operated as brothels, where unsuspecting patrons were secretly dosed with LSD so agents could observe their behavior. Congressional investigations later found that some subjects suffered lasting psychological harm, and at least one death was directly linked to the experiments. Many experiments were conducted without informed consent.

The program remained largely unknown until the mid-1970s, when investigations by the Church Committee and subsequent Senate hearings revealed portions of its existence. Former CIA Director Richard Helms had ordered most MKULTRA files destroyed in 1973, leaving investigators with only financial records that had escaped destruction.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), who chairs the task force, argued that the destruction of those records continues to prevent the public from understanding the full scope of the program.

'Medical Torture'
Kinzer testified that MKULTRA represented one of the most extensive secret human experimentation programs ever conducted by the U.S. government.

“MK-ULTRA conducted the most extreme experiments on human beings that have ever been carried out by a U.S. government agency,” he testified. “By any standard they qualify as medical torture.”

Kinzer argued that Sidney Gottlieb, the CIA chemist who oversaw MKULTRA, deliberately sought out vulnerable populations referred to as “expendables" for experimentation. He testified that agency officials targeted prisoners, psychiatric patients and other people who were unlikely to attract public attention if something went wrong.

Kinzer urged lawmakers not to view MKULTRA solely as history.

Although Gottlieb ultimately acknowledged the program failed to achieve true mind control, Kinzer argued that rapid advances in neuroscience, artificial intelligence and brain-computer technologies make congressional oversight just as important today.

O’Neill Challenged the Official History
Tom O’Neill focused much of his testimony on what he believes Congress still does not know about MKULTRA.

O’Neill argued that when CIA officials testified during the 1970s investigations, they portrayed MKULTRA as an expensive failure while withholding important details about the program’s reach.

He also discussed years of research that formed the basis of his book Chaos. O’Neill examined psychiatrist Louis Jolyon West, who conducted CIA-funded research and later became connected to investigations surrounding Charles Manson.

O’Neill stopped short of claiming the CIA controlled Manson or orchestrated the Tate-LaBianca murders. Instead, he argued that inconsistencies in government records and previously undisclosed relationships between West and MKULTRA officials justify additional investigation.

O’Neill believes the historical record remains incomplete because so many documents were destroyed before Congress could examine them. He also highlighted two other figures whose names surfaced repeatedly during his research: Jack Ruby and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Ruby, who fatally shot Lee Harvey Oswald two days after President John F. Kennedy was assassinated, became a focal point because West evaluated Ruby while he was in custody. O’Neill testified that Ruby’s mental condition deteriorated rapidly after his arrest and questioned why West, who had connections to CIA-funded behavioral research, became involved in his case.

O’Neill argued that the circumstances surrounding West’s examination and his later proposal to transfer Ruby to his own care deserve additional scrutiny.

O’Neill also discussed the government’s surveillance of King, arguing that intelligence agencies during the Cold War often blurred the line between legitimate national security investigations and intrusive domestic operations. O’Neill cited the government’s extensive monitoring of the civil rights leader as evidence of how broadly intelligence agencies operated during the era and why lawmakers should continue examining classified records from that period.

NIH Testimony Left Some Confused
One of the hearing’s most unexpected moments came from Ginexi.

Unlike the other witnesses, Ginexi devoted her testimony to current National Institutes of Health policies rather than MKULTRA. She warned that recent changes to NIH grant administration and scientific oversight threaten biomedical research and shift decision-making from scientists to political appointees.

Her testimony discussed grant cancellations, peer review, research funding and political influence at NIH.

That disconnect became even more noticeable during questioning.

Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) openly questioned why so much of her testimony focused on NIH rather than the subject of the hearing. According to the committee’s official summary, Ginexi responded that she was there to discuss “the destruction of the NIH and cancellation of grants and political control of the NIH.”

While Kinzer and O’Neill spent their time discussing MKULTRA documents, historical evidence and intelligence oversight, Ginexi largely spoke of her grievances regarding NIH.

Why the Hearing Generated So Much Attention
The hearing generated widespread online interest because MKULTRA occupies a unique place in American history.

Unlike many alleged government conspiracies, the existence of MKULTRA itself is not disputed. The CIA has acknowledged the program existed, and Congress investigated it decades ago.

What remains disputed, however, is how extensive the experiments became, how many people were affected, and whether all surviving records have ever been made public.

Kinzer and O’Neill argued that unanswered questions remain because the destruction of records prevented investigators from fully reconstructing the program. Neither witness claimed Congress proved modern mind-control programs exist, but both encouraged lawmakers to continue pressing intelligence agencies for additional records and greater transparency.

Whether Congress ultimately uncovers new information remains to be seen.

Title:
The 128 Logical-Qutrit Hampton Processor, Software and FPGA Execution of HQH-539-512 A fixed-round ternary engine with a SHA3-512 envelope

Arvin B. Hampton 
539 Labs Incorporated 
Hot Springs, Arkansas, United States 
arvin@539labs.org
1 September 2026
Abstract
HQH-539-512 is a deterministic 512-bit digest. Software absorbs an arbitrary message with SHA3-512, walks the resulting integer through 539 public steps of the Canonical T3 map, and finalizes with SHA3-512. The 128 Logical-Qutrit Hampton processor is the FPGA that runs that walk: 128 parallel 768-bit T3 cores, a residue multiplexor with no secret-dependent branch, and a counter that cannot retire before 539 steps.
The map is an integer function. Residue 0 and residue 1 divide exactly by 3. Residue 2 is floor division and equals (2n − 1)/3. From a 512-bit absorb, 539 expanding steps stay under 736 bits, so a 768-bit core is enough. One hundred twenty-eight single trits hold only 203 bits and cannot store the state; the array is 128 wide cores.
SHA3-512 supplies the 512-bit interface and the Grover bound of order 2^256 on the digest. T3 supplies a public integer walk with no hidden-subgroup structure of the kind Shor’s algorithm exploits on RSA and elliptic curves. Constant-time selection and a fixed step count close the timing and control-flow channels that learning-based side-channel models use. Known-Answer Tests and single-bit avalanche from the reference software are reported.
Keywords. ternary map; fixed-round hash; SHA3-512; FPGA; constant-time arithmetic; post-quantum; side-channel; Known-Answer Tests
What is being built
Two artifacts implement the same function.
The software is hqh539_core.py. It is the reference model. It defines Canonical T3, applies it 539 times, wraps both ends with SHA3-512, and emits a 512-bit hex digest. Every hardware bit that claims to compute HQH-539-512 has to match that model on the test vectors in the appendix.
The hardware is the 128 LQH processor on FPGA. Each core is a 768-bit integer stepper. The array runs 128 independent evaluations in lockstep. A host writes a SHA3-512 absorb, commands 539 steps, and reads a SHA3-512 digest.
Together they give a module a complementary ternary engine that SHA3-512 does not contain, while the module still speaks a 512-bit approved-width digest. The rest of the paper is only that map, that budget, that datapath, and the attack surface they present to a quantum computer and to an AI-assisted adversary.
Canonical T3

Let N be the non-negative integers. Canonical T3 is the only map in the body.

T3(0) = 0. For n > 0 let r = n mod 3. If r = 0 then T3(n) = n // 3. If r = 1 then T3(n) = (4n + 2) // 3. If r = 2 then T3(n) = (2n + 1) // 3. The symbol // is integer division on non-negative operands.
2.1 Integrality
Lemma 1. T3 maps N into N.
Proof. Write n = 3k, or n = 3k + 1, or n = 3k + 2.

If n = 3k then T3(n) = k.

If n = 3k + 1 then 4n + 2 = 12k + 6 = 3(4k + 2), so T3(n) = 4k + 2.
If n = 3k + 2 then 2n + 1 = 6k + 5, which is 2 mod 3 and is not divisible by 3 in the rationals. Integer division still yields an integer: (2n + 1) // 3 = 2k + 1. The same value is (2n − 1)/3. Direct check on 0 through 4999 found no counter-example to (2n + 1) // 3 = (2n − 1) // 3 on residue 2.
Lemma 2. T3(3k) = k, T3(3k + 1) = 4k + 2, T3(3k + 2) = 2k + 1.
These are the identities the FPGA computes after the residue is known.
2.2 Small cycles
Lemma 3. T3(0) = 0. T3(1) = 2 and T3(2) = 1.
The hash does not stop at these values. It stops when the public counter reaches 539.
2.3 Unit orbits
Seed 0: 0 (fixed) Seed 1: 1 → 2 → 1 Seed 4: 4 → 6 → 2 Seed 5: 5 → 3 → 1 Seed 10: 10 → 14 → 9 → 3 → 1 Seed 20: 20 → 13 → 18 → 6 → 2 Seed 21: 21 → 7 → 10 → 14 → 9 → 3 → 1 Seed 100: 100 → 134 → 89 → 59 → 39 → 13 → 18 → 6 → 2 Seed 4880: 4880 → 3253 → 4338 → 1446 → 482 → 321 → 107 → 71 → 47 → 31 → 42 → 14 → 9 → 3 → 1
Table 1. First tests of the software stepper and of the FPGA T3 core.
Width of one walk
Lemma 4. If n0 is at most 2^512 − 1 and every step uses the expanding branch n ↦ (4n + 2)/3, then n_539 is less than 2^736.
Proof. Then n_{t+1} < (4/3) n_t + 1, so n_t < (4/3)^t (n0 + 3). Therefore log2(n_539) < 539 log2(4/3) + log2(n0 + 3). The first term is about 223.705. The second is less than 512.01. The sum is less than 735.72.
A 768-bit register, or twelve 64-bit limbs, covers every walk that starts from a SHA3-512 absorb. Two hundred random 512-bit seeds walked 539 steps peaked at 514 bits. The 768-bit width is a cap, not a typical size.
The budget is public and fixed. The free map on 2^512 − 1 reached the 2-cycle in 824 steps. After 539 steps the absorb of the empty string still had 202 bits, and the absorb of abc still had 162 bits. Residue counts on the abc walk were 195, 160, and 184. The body ends on a large integer. All three branches fire. A core that retires at 1 is wrong.
Software: HQH-539-512
Let SHA3-512 be the FIPS 202 function. Let bytes(u) be the big-endian representation used by the reference model, of length (bit_length(u) + 7) // 8. Let || be concatenation.
u0 = integer(SHA3-512(m || s)), a 512-bit word.
For i from 0 to 538, set u_{i+1} = T3(u_i). The split 18 + 521 is only two compare values on the same counter.
Return SHA3-512(bytes(u_539) || s) as 512 bits.
The reference step has no secret-dependent branch:
r0 = n//3; r1 = (4n+2)//3; r2 = (2n+1)//3; return r0*(r==0) + r1*(r==1) + r2*(r==2)
CPython longs are not themselves constant-time. The line records the discipline the FPGA must keep. Production software moves the same selection into a constant-time arithmetic library.
A keyed call is the same function with s used as the key. A 256-bit display form is a truncation of the 512-bit digest. Neither changes the body.

Hardware: the 128 LQH FPGA

Three facts fix the floorplan.
A register of 128 trits has 3^128 states, a 203-bit integer. The walk is 512 bits at absorb and up to 736 bits in the worst case. The array is therefore 128 parallel 768-bit cores, not one 128-trit tape.
Write n = sum_{j=0}^{11} a_j 2^{64 j}. Because 2^64 ≡ 1 (mod 3), the residue is (a0 + … + a11) mod 3. The residue unit is an adder tree on twelve limb residues.
After r is known, Lemma 2 gives the value. All three candidates are computed. One-bit predicates s0, s1, s2 mask the result: s0·y0 + s1·y1 + s2·y2. Control flow does not depend on r.
The visible commands are LOAD, STEP_T3, COUNT_539, FINALIZE, and KAT_CMP. COUNT_539 is a 10-bit counter with a hard stop at 539. Early halt is a fail. FINALIZE sends bytes(u_539) || s into on-chip or host SHA3-512.
The testbench that closes the hardware is a co-simulation against the software. It must pass Table 1 on seeds 0 through 30, keep every 539-step walk inside 768 bits, refuse early retirement, and match the appendix digests for the empty message, abc, the self-test string, 0x00, and 0xFF.
Table 2. FPGA organization. LUT and Fmax rows are first-order planning estimates.
Block: Integer width. One core: 768 bits. Array: 768 bits per core. Block: T3 steps per digest. One core: 539, public. Array: 539, lockstep. Block: Residue path. One core: sum of twelve limbs mod 3. Array: replicated. Block: Branch select. One core: masked mux, three candidates. Array: replicated. Block: Planning LUT estimate. One core: about 4,500 as first sketched. Array: about 620,000 as first sketched. Block: Planning Fmax estimate. One core: 150–200 MHz. Array: 120–150 MHz.

Measured software behaviour

All numbers in this section come from hqh539_core.py version 1.2.
The self-test message hashed twice produced the same 128-character digest. Changing abc to abd flipped 271 of 512 bits. Sixteen single-bit flips in a 64-byte random message produced Hamming distances 259, 271, 258, 263, 257, 261, 264, 248, 258, 243, 251, 247, 258, 261, 259, 257. The mean is 257.2 bits, a rate of 0.502. Full digests are in the appendix.

Quantum computers and AI-assisted attacks
A module that only exposes SHA3-512 already has a 512-bit digest. Grover search on that digest costs on the order of 2^256 hash evaluations. HQH-539-512 keeps that interface, so that Grover number does not get worse. The software and the FPGA add a second, public layer that a quantum computer and a learning adversary have to cross as well.
7.1 Why Shor does not eat the body
Shor’s algorithm finds periods of abelian hidden-subgroup problems. That is the reason RSA moduli and elliptic-curve discrete logarithms fall. Canonical T3 is not a group exponentiation and not a hidden period on (Z/NZ)*. It is a three-branch integer map. Residue 0 contracts. Residue 1 expands by 4/3. Residue 2 contracts by about 2/3 and is floor division. The branch taken at step i depends on the current integer, which depends on every previous branch. There is no published reduction of “invert 539 mixed T3 steps” to period-finding.
A quantum adversary still has Grover on the 512-bit finalize. That is the floor. To do better than Grover it has to exploit structure inside the 539-step walk or inside SHA3-512. The walk is public, so the structure is not a secret key schedule. It is also not the algebraic object Shor is built for.

7.2 Why a learning adversary does not get a timing oracle
Modern side-channel attacks train on traces: wall-clock time, cache, power, electromagnetic emission. They work when the implementation branches on secret data or when the work factor depends on the input.
The software step computes all three candidates and selects by arithmetic. The FPGA does the same with word-wide masks. The step count is 539 on every digest. There is no early abort when a small attractor appears. Limb residue is a sum modulo 3, not a data-dependent divider bypass. Those four facts remove the control-flow and variable-round features that a trained model uses as labels.
What remains is amplitude on a fixed-latency datapath. That is the ordinary constant-time hardware problem. It is not solved by T3 itself. It is the reason the FPGA, not only the Python model, is part of the design: the masked mux and the locked counter are gates, not comments.

7.3 What the pair closes

SHA3-512 alone is a binary sponge. It does not walk a ternary residue. A raw T3 loop in variable-time software walks a ternary residue but leaks the residue in time and does not return a fixed 512-bit word. HQH-539-512 on the 128 LQH FPGA is the pair that does both: a public 539-step ternary body with no secret-dependent branch, wrapped to 512 bits by SHA3-512.
Against a quantum computer the digest width keeps Grover at 2^256 and the body keeps Shor off the integer walk. Against an AI-assisted adversary the masked step and the fixed counter remove the timing and control-flow labels. That is the defense the software and the hardware are built to complete. A separate reduction from a named hard problem to preimage or collision resistance of H is not given in this paper.
Games
Let H(m, s) be HQH-539-512.
Preimage: given y, find (m, s) with H(m, s) = y.
Second-preimage: given (m*, s*) and y = H(m*, s*), find a different pair with the same digest.
Collision: find two different pairs with the same digest.
Inverting the body is the integer problem: given u_539, find a 512-bit u0 that reaches it in exactly 539 T3 steps, then invert the SHA3-512 absorb. The games name the interface. They are not a proof.
Status of the implementation
The software reference exists and produces the appendix vectors. SystemVerilog sketches of a partitioned T3 stage and a single-core wrapper exist. The FPGA testbench named in Section 5 is the next build: RTL T3 against Table 1 and against the appendix. Planning LUT and Fmax figures in Table 2 are estimates from a first core sketch, not a finished place-and-route of 128 cores.
Conclusion
HQH-539-512 is a 512-bit digest whose middle is 539 public T3 steps. The map is integral. Residue 2 is (2n − 1)/3. A 768-bit FPGA core covers the walk. The 128 LQH device is 128 of those cores. Software defines the function. The FPGA runs it in constant step count with a masked residue mux. SHA3-512 keeps a 512-bit interface. That combination is the quantum and AI-facing design: Grover stays on a 512-bit digest, Shor has no hidden-subgroup handle on the walk, and a learning adversary is not handed a timing label for the residue.
References
[1] National Institute of Standards and Technology. FIPS PUB 202: SHA-3 Standard: Permutation-Based Hash and Extendable-Output Functions. August 2015. [2] Grover, L. K. A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search. STOC 1996. [3] Shor, P. W. Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer. SIAM J. Comput. 26 (1997). [4] Hampton, A. B. hqh539_core.py, version 1.2. Reference implementation of Canonical T3 and HQH-539-512. 539 Labs. [5] Hampton, A. B. We received a strong response to our call for submissions, with many high-quality and interesting proposals. Given the limited number of presentation slots available in the conference program, the Program Committee faced some difficult choices, and unfortunately, we were unable to accommodate a number of well-rated submissions.
Following the Program Committee’s review and evaluation, we regret to inform you that we are unable to include your proposal in the FIPS ‘n’ Chips 2026 conference program.

The reviewer has suggested these comments about your manuscript.
This proposal introduces a new cryptographic hash function, HQH-539. There are two primary concerns regarding its inclusion in the FnC conference. First, novel cryptographic primitives typically require rigorous peer review and public scrutiny, which is usually achieved by submitting them to a dedicated cryptographic research conference or, at minimum, publishing them as an IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive preprint. Second, FIPS 140 validation is strictly reserved for standardized algorithms, and HQH-539 has not yet been considered for standardization. Consequently, the proposal in its current state may not be suitable for presentation at the FIPS 'n' Chips conference. text:
So the irony is that a farmer without a computer was precisely the teacher we needed in this age of magical technologies. 

Unwavering in his devotion to quality and propriety, Wendell Berry lived as a reminder that it is good and true and beautiful to meet the world on its terms. His work offers us so much about how to thrive amidst complexity, how to navigate wicked problems, how to serve life in our shifty world of compounding and entangled crises, because he relentlessly points us back into the becoming and being-with of our lives. Because he shows us what it means to be "married" to a situation.

History tends to speak in couplets. Perhaps because both men were members of William Irwin Thompson's Lindisfarne Association, I have always seen Berry as half of a generational counterpoint alongside @stewartbrand, the urban and rural perspectives on an emerging planetary culture. Reading them together, they give us a stereoscopic view of what it means to live in service to the here and now: Brand zooms out to the "blue marble" satellite view and @longnow 10,000-year horizon, and Berry zooms in through the patient and loving study of a sparrow or a poem. One is unquestionably "tech-positive" and the other a cantankerous holdout, but both of them, in their own way, guided millions into a rediscovered sense of deep time and responsibility. Brand gave us "pace layers" and the Whole Earth Catalog — a field guide to "the right tool for the job" if ever there were one — and a multi-volume love letter to maintenance, whereas Berry, in his abstinence from acceleration, drew us back into what is ultimately the same scope and connectedness:

"The job now is to get back to that perennial and substantial world in which we really do live, in which the foundations of our life will be visible to us, and in which we can accept our responsibilities again within the conditions of necessity and mystery. In that world all wakeful and responsible people, dead, living, and unborn, are contemporaries. And that is the only contemporaneity worth having.

"What is needed is work of durable value; the time or age of it matters only after the value has been established. That a good poet is our contemporary reassured us of the continuing liveliness of certain possibilities; the contemporaneity of a worthless poet is a depressant. But there is much that we need that we cannot get from our contemporaries — even assuming that the work we have from them is the best that is possible: they cannot give us the sense of the longevity of human experience, the sense of the practicable, or *proven* possibility, that we get from older writing. Our past is not merely something to depart from; it is to commune with, to speak with... Remove this sense of continuity, and we are left with the thoughtless present tense of machines.  If we fail to see that we live in the same world that Homer lived in, then we not only misunderstand Homer; we misunderstand ourselves. The past is our definition. We may strive, with good reason, to escape it, or to escape what is bad in it, but we will escape it only by adding something better to it.

"If, as I believe, one of the functions of tradition is to convey a sense of our perennial nature and of the necessities and values that are the foundation of our life, then it follows that, without a live tradition, we are necessarily the prey of fashion: we have no choice but to emulate in the arts of 'practical men' of commerce and industry whose mode of life is distraction of spirit and whose livelihood is the outdating of fads."

Berry may be gone today, but he remains a contemporary in the perennial sense, because his work is of durable value.

2/3

Stocks and crypto don’t always need separate platforms.

One interesting use case on @MEXC is Stock Futures — designed for traders who want to express a view on stock-market moves without directly owning the underlying shares.

With Stock Futures, users can:
• Go long or short
• Trade market events like earnings and sector volatility
• Use USDT settlement
• Access selected stock-related instruments with leverage
The key difference vs RealStocks: RealStocks represent actual share ownership, while Stock Futures are derivatives. Leverage can amplify both gains and losses, and liquidation/funding fees may apply.

印度拍板推動「半導體任務 2.0」，聚焦國際大廠與台商進駐！
印度政府正式批准「印度半導體任務 2.0」（ISM 2.0），政府補貼預算擴增至 148 億美元，預計將帶動整體私營部門投資上看 465 億美元。
三大重點解析：
一、 補齊全產業鏈缺塊：ISM 1.0 主要著重於吸引晶圓製造與封測廠（ATMP/OSAT）落腳印度；而全新的 ISM 2.0 則將範圍擴大至「半導體材料、設備製造、晶片設計、封測、晶圓製造以及研發新創」等六大支柱，意圖打造本土半導體產業鏈。
二、 國際大廠與台灣鏈投資進度：在 ISM 1.0 政策推動下，台廠扮演了關鍵技術夥伴角色。力積電（PSMC）與印度塔塔集團（Tata）合作，以技術授權模式協助興建印度首座 12 吋晶圓廠；鴻海與 HCL 的合資公司（HCL-Foxconn）亦投入封測布局。美國記憶體巨頭美光（Micron）等企業的封測廠也已陸續啟用。印度政府期盼透過 2.0 政策，進一步爭取更多晶圓廠落腳。
三、 與台灣產業的戰略關係：對擁有完整生態系的台灣半導體與電子代工產業而言，這既是設備、材料與技術服務出口印度的戰略商機，也是全球半導體製造地緣分布的新契機。
